newsitem.title: CHINA: China remembers Mao, forgets his class struggles.
newsitem.headline: China remembers Mao, forgets his class struggles.

text.p: Dead for two decades, Mao Zedong peered out from the front pages of Chinese newspapers on Monday when state publishers issued three new volumes of his poems and letters to mark the 20th anniversary of his death.

Thousands of Chinese formed a 300-metre (1,000-ft) queue under the scorching sun for a glimpse of the embalmed body of the Great Helmsman, lying in a crystal coffin at a mausoleum on Tiananmen Square in the heart of the Chinese capital, Beijing.

The ruling Communist Party paid its tribute to the father of new China with the publication of a collection of Mao's poems, a biography and letters he wrote to friends and relatives in his birthplace, Shaoshan in central Hunan province.

Newspapers splashed across their front pages the news of the publication of the third to fifth volumes of the "Collected Works of Mao Zedong" illustrated with a photograph of the leader in his prime, but made no mention of Mao's now-defunct policies of endless proletarian revolution.
"What the Communist Party is telling the people is clear -- read his poems and letters, but forget his class struggles and ultra-left policies," said a Chinese analyst who asked not to be identified.

Mao's death on September 9, 1976, provided the opportunity for current paramount leader Deng Xiaoping to bounce back from the political wilderness and reverse just about everything that Mao stood for.

Almost two decades of economic reforms launched by Deng have set Chinese free to make money and liberated the country from Mao's ideological chains. Deng coined the phrase: "To get rich is glorious," a slogan that would have caused Mao, a devout Marxist, to turn in his grave.
The Communist Party has discreetly kept Mao enshrined on China's political altar.

"If Mao Zedong fell, the Communist Party would be in a dangerous position," Xu Youyu, an academic researching his ultra-leftist (1966-76) Cultural Revolution, said in reference to the ideological credibility of the party.

Mao has retained his halo because the Communist Party, in power since 1949, cannot denounce all his atrocities without undermining its own position. Even Deng, who fell from Mao's graces twice in the Cultural Revolution, summed up Mao as 70 percent right and 30 percent wrong.
Mao, who launched the catastrophic Great Leap Forward in 1958 that starved 28 million Chinese to death in a man-made famine, is still respectfully known to millions simply as "chairman".
"Mao Zedong is a weapon of the Communist Party," Xu said.
Mao had envisioned a leap in economic growth that would allow China to surpass Western powers and urged farmers to abandon their fields and join a rush to make steel in backyard furnaces.
During his tumultuous Cultural Revolution schools were closed and radical Red Guards stormed temples and homes to destroy any remnants of bourgeois tradition.
Two decades after Mao's death, Chinese are far wealthier but many are nostalgic for Mao because of a widening gap between rich and poor, soaring crime and widespread corruption.
"I come here almost every year...I will forever cherish the memory of chairman Mao," said 64-year-old retired government employee Yao Heng after a tour of Mao's mausoleum.
"He committed mistakes but his motives were not wrong and were for the people," Yao said after glimpsing Mao's waxlike embalmed body.
